newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Continuing signs of risks to inflation-Irish C.Ban.
newsitem.headline: Continuing signs of risks to inflation-Irish C.Ban.

text.p: Ireland's Central Bank said on Thursday that although most concurrent indicators of inflation are relatively stable, there were continuing signs of increasing risks for inflation.

"Taking into account the 1997 budget stimulus to domestic demand and the offsetting effect of an appreciating nominal effective exchange rate, the headline rate of consumer price inflation is expected to average about 2.3 percent in 1997," the bank said in its quarterly bulletin.
Personal consumer expenditure is forecast to grow by five percent in real terms during 1997, underpinned by buoyant consumer confidence and improved labour market conditions, the bank said.

The growth in investment expenditure is also forecast to continue while building and construction investment, driven in part by continued household formation, is expected to grow by about eight percent in volume terms.
The bank said the outlook is also for a pick-up in Irish export growth while the greatly improved performance of the labour market is expected to continue although at a moderately slower pace.

It expects total employment gains of about 35,000 in 1997 on top of an estimated rise of 49,000 last year while unemployment is expected to fall by 6,000, bringing the jobless rate down to about 11.5 percent.
Overall, Irish GNP is expected to grow by around 5.5 percent, a modest deceleration from an estimated 6.0 percent in 1996.

The central bank said the level of general government debt is expected to fall to about 69 percent of GDP by end-1997, reflecting the current strength of economic growth and the relatively low level of interest rates.
